newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: EU entry still a priority for Slovenia - analysts.
newsitem.headline: EU entry still a priority for Slovenia - analysts.

text.p: European Union entry will remain Slovenia's chief goal, despite the resignation of Foreign Minister Zoran Thaler following opposition criticism of his handling of Europe and NATO, analysts said on Friday.

"There will be no change in Slovenia's orientation towards the European Union because Slovenia is already firmly open to the EU," France Krizanic, a researcher at the Economic Institute at Ljubljana University's Law Faculty, told Reuters.
Thaler, 35, quit over what he called "impossible" domestic political conditions and lack of unity among parties on issues of national importance, like joining the EU and NATO.
The opposition accused Thaler of mishandling negotiations on membership of these international organisations.
Analysts said Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek's centre-left Liberal Democrats should have no problem replacing Thaler with another pro-European minister.
"Thaler is replaceable and the current coalition will definitely choose a new man who will continue with the European policy," political analyst Miha Kovac said.
"It is not serious for a foreign minister to resign after five months in office, since he should have been able to handle party disputes," he said.
The resignation was not likely to have much impact on Slovenia's international relations but could give opposition parties further cause to criticise the government, he added.
Thaler has served as foreign minister since February when a new government was formed following an inconclusive general election in November.

It is the second time Thaler has lost his job as foreign minister in the past 15 months. He was forced out of office in a parliamentary confidence vote in May 1996 after being accused of botching Slovenia's bid for associate membership of the EU.
The association agreement was finally signed in June 1996.
Some analysts speculated that Thaler was made a scapegoat for his party after Slovenia was left out of the first round of NATO expansion.

"Although Slovenia made it to the EU that does not balance out its failure to be included in NATO in spite of a very strong campaign that lasted several months," said an analyst who declined to be named. "The party needed to find someone to blame for that," he added.
Last month the European Commission recommended that Slovenia should be included in the first round of EU enlargement, along with Estonia, Cyprus, Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
The NATO alliance invited only the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland to join, leaving out Slovenia and Romania.

The Liberal Democrats said they had asked Thaler to reconsider but that they would name a new candidate for the post of foreign minister in September if he declined. Thaler will remain in the office until then.
